dna_intro_ladder.display_text: DNA is a polymer with a remarkably regular structure. Two sugar-phosphate backbones run alongside each other, connected by rungs made of paired nitrogenous bases.
dna_intro_ladder.llm_text: DNA is a polymer with a remarkably regular structure. Two sugar-phosphate backbones run alongside each other, connected by rungs made of paired nitrogenous bases.
dna_intro_ladder.spoken_text: DNA is a polymer with a remarkably regular structure. Two sugar-phosphate backbones run alongside each other, connected by rungs made of paired nitrogenous bases.

dna_base_color_code.display_text: Each rung is made of two bases meeting in the middle: adenine in red, thymine in blue, guanine in yellow, cytosine in green. Notice how each base only pairs with one partner.
dna_base_color_code.llm_text: Each rung is made of two bases meeting in the middle: adenine in red, thymine in blue, guanine in yellow, cytosine in green. Notice how each base only pairs with one partner.

ladder_to_helix_twist.display_text: Now watch as the flat ladder twists into its real three-dimensional shape: the double helix. The backbones spiral around a shared axis, and the base pairs stack like steps on the interior.
ladder_to_helix_twist.llm_text: Now watch as the flat ladder twists into its real three-dimensional shape: the double helix. The backbones spiral around a shared axis, and the base pairs stack like steps on the interior.
ladder_to_helix_twist.spoken_text: Now watch as the flat ladder twists into its real three-dimensional shape: the double helix. The backbones spiral around a shared axis, and the base pairs stack like steps on the interior.

helix_turn_periodicity.display_text: One full turn of the helix spans about ten base pairs. You can toggle between the schematic ladder and this realistic helix at any time to build your mental map between the two views.

antiparallel_arrows_intro.display_text: Arrows along each backbone show the direction of the strand: one points up, the other points down. These directions refer to the carbon atoms of the sugar ring at each end.
antiparallel_arrows_intro.llm_text: Arrows along each backbone show the direction of the strand: one points up, the other points down. These directions refer to the carbon atoms of the sugar ring at each end.
antiparallel_arrows_intro.spoken_text: Arrows along each backbone show the direction of the strand: one points up, the other points down. These directions refer to the carbon atoms of the sugar ring at each end.

antiparallel_explanation.display_text: The two strands always run in opposite directions. This antiparallel arrangement isn't optional — it's forced by the directional chemistry of the sugar-phosphate backbone. Try rotating the helix to confirm the arrows from any angle.
antiparallel_explanation.llm_text: The two strands always run in opposite directions. This antiparallel arrangement isn't optional — it's forced by the directional chemistry of the sugar-phosphate backbone. Try rotating the helix to confirm the arrows from any angle.

base_pairing_activity_intro.display_text: Here is a template strand reading 5' to 3': A-T-G-C-C-A-G-T. On the right is an empty backbone waiting for its complementary bases. Drag bases from the palette below to complete the pairing — remember, A pairs with T, and G pairs with C.
base_pairing_activity_intro.llm_text: Here is a template strand reading five prime to three prime: A, T, G, C, C, A, G, T. On the right is an empty backbone waiting for its complementary bases. Drag bases from the palette below to complete the pairing — remember, A pairs with T, and G pairs with C.
base_pairing_activity_intro.spoken_text: Here is a template strand reading five prime to three prime: A, T, G, C, C, A, G, T. On the right is an empty backbone waiting for its complementary bases. Drag bases from the palette below to complete the pairing — remember, A pairs with T, and G pairs with C.

base_pairing_activity_complete.display_text: Well done — the completed strand reads 3'-TACGGTCA-5', running opposite to the template. Notice that A-T pairs form two hydrogen bonds while G-C pairs form three, making G-C pairs slightly stronger.
base_pairing_activity_complete.llm_text: Well done — the completed strand reads three prime dash T, A, C, G, G, T, C, A dash five prime, running opposite to the template. Notice that A-T pairs form two hydrogen bonds while G-C pairs form three, making G-C pairs slightly stronger.
base_pairing_activity_complete.spoken_text: Well done — the completed strand reads three prime dash T, A, C, G, G, T, C, A dash five prime, running opposite to the template. Notice that A-T pairs form two hydrogen bonds while G-C pairs form three, making G-C pairs slightly stronger.

helicase_intro.display_text: Meet helicase, the first enzyme at the replication fork. It breaks the hydrogen bonds between paired bases, unwinding the double helix and exposing the two strands so they can serve as templates.
helicase_intro.llm_text: Meet helicase, the first enzyme at the replication fork. It breaks the hydrogen bonds between paired bases, unwinding the double helix and exposing the two strands so they can serve as templates.
helicase_intro.spoken_text: Meet helicase, the first enzyme at the replication fork. It breaks the hydrogen bonds between paired bases, unwinding the double helix and exposing the two strands so they can serve as templates.

ssb_intro.display_text: As helicase separates the strands, single-strand binding proteins, or SSBs, attach behind it. Single strands of DNA are unstable and tend to re-pair or fold on themselves — the SSBs hold them open and accessible for replication.
ssb_intro.llm_text: As helicase separates the strands, single-strand binding proteins, or S S Bs, attach behind it. Single strands of DNA are unstable and tend to re-pair or fold on themselves — the S S Bs hold them open and accessible for replication.

leading_strand_synthesis.display_text: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the 3' end of a growing strand, so it travels along its template in the 3'-to-5' direction, building the new strand 5' to 3'. On this template, that direction matches the moving fork — so polymerase can synthesize continuously. It needs a starting primer to begin, but once going, it doesn't stop.
leading_strand_synthesis.llm_text: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the three prime end of a growing strand, so it travels along its template in the three prime to five prime direction, building the new strand five prime to three prime. On this template, that direction matches the moving fork — so polymerase can synthesize continuously. It needs a starting primer to begin, but once going, it doesn't stop.
leading_strand_synthesis.spoken_text: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the three prime end of a growing strand, so it travels along its template in the three prime to five prime direction, building the new strand five prime to three prime. On this template, that direction matches the moving fork — so polymerase can synthesize continuously. It needs a starting primer to begin, but once going, it doesn't stop.

lagging_strand_fragments.display_text: On this template, the fork moves away from polymerase's required direction of travel, so it can't synthesize continuously. Instead, it works backward in short bursts, producing Okazaki fragments, then jumps back near the fork to start the next fragment.
lagging_strand_fragments.llm_text: On this template, the fork moves away from polymerase's required direction of travel, so it can't synthesize continuously. Instead, it works backward in short bursts, producing Okazaki fragments, then jumps back near the fork to start the next fragment.

ligase_seals_fragments.display_text: Now DNA ligase arrives and seals the gaps between the Okazaki fragments, joining them into one continuous lagging strand.
ligase_seals_fragments.llm_text: Now DNA ligase arrives and seals the gaps between the Okazaki fragments, joining them into one continuous lagging strand.
ligase_seals_fragments.spoken_text: Now DNA ligase arrives and seals the gaps between the Okazaki fragments, joining them into one continuous lagging strand.

full_fork_summary.display_text: Here is the complete replication fork: helicase unwinding at the front, SSBs holding the strands open, polymerase synthesizing the leading strand continuously, polymerase building Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand, and ligase sealing them behind. Because the two template strands run in opposite directions and polymerase can only build 5' to 3', the two new strands must be made differently. This asymmetry is a direct consequence of the antiparallel structure you saw earlier.

Because the two template strands run in opposite directions and polymerase can only build five prime to three prime, the two new strands must be made differently. This asymmetry is a direct consequence of the antiparallel structure you saw earlier.

semiconservative_round_one.display_text: This parental DNA molecule is rendered entirely in gold to mark the original material. Watch as it replicates: the strands separate, new complementary strands are synthesized in silver, producing two daughter molecules — each with one gold strand and one silver strand. This is what makes replication semiconservative: every daughter conserves one original parental strand.

semiconservative_prediction_prompt.display_text: Now these two daughter molecules will each replicate again. Before we play it out — predict the composition of the four resulting molecules: will all four be half gold and half silver, will two be hybrid and two be fully silver, or will all four be fully silver?
semiconservative_prediction_prompt.llm_text: Now these two daughter molecules will each replicate again. semiconservative_round_two_reveal.display_text: Here is round two: each daughter molecule separates and synthesizes a new silver strand. The result is four molecules — two are hybrids with one gold and one silver strand, and two are fully silver, containing no original parental material. This pattern of hybrid and fully-new molecules is exactly the signature that confirmed DNA replication is semiconservative rather than conservative or dispersive.

lab_recap_summary.display_text: Let's recap what we've covered: the double-helix structure with its sugar-phosphate backbones and bases; complementary base-pairing rules with hydrogen-bond counts; the antiparallel, 5'-to-3' arrangement of the two strands; the action of helicase, SSBs, polymerase, and ligase at the replication fork; the leading and lagging strand asymmetry with Okazaki fragments; and the semiconservative nature of replication.
